tldr: The authors developed "SoTa," a soft, durable capacitive tactile skin that costs under $10 in materials, fits the full hands of both humans and robots, and shares a common 202-taxel layout. By aligning tactile correspondences directly in hardware, easily collected human demonstrations can be integrated into robot imitation learning without cross-sensor mapping, more than doubling policy success on unseen objects and environments.
hero_caption: Overview of the SoTa-based data collection system. (a) On the robot side, teleoperation using a Meta Quest and Rokoko glove records images, tactile signals, and joint commands at 30 Hz. (b) On the human side, wearing a fabric glove with the identical tactile skin in front of a camera enables collecting large amounts of visuo-tactile demonstrations without using a robot.
overview:
In dexterous manipulation with multi-fingered hands, tactile feedback is essential for capturing contacts that occur in visual blind spots. However, the scarcity of visuo-tactile data has been a major bottleneck for robot learning. Teleoperating dexterous robot hands requires expensive equipment and is time-consuming, whereas human manipulation demonstrations are far cheaper and easier to collect at scale. To leverage human data for robot learning, however, sensors must conform to hands of varying shapes and sizes, cover the full hand, and produce corresponding tactile signals across embodiments.

To address this challenge, the authors introduce "SoTa," a soft capacitive tactile skin fabricated for under $10 in raw materials per skin. Using laser-micromachined conductive fabric electrodes, the skin's geometry is customized to fit both human and robot hands while maintaining an identical functional layout of 202 sensor elements (taxels) across the fingers and palm. Thanks to this hardware alignment, both human and robot tactile signals can be processed with a shared tactile encoder without learning complex cross-sensor mappings.

In real-world robot experiments, the authors evaluated three contact-rich manipulation tasks: box reorientation, cup picking from a stack, and plug insertion into a wall outlet. Adding human demonstrations as auxiliary training alongside a fixed budget of robot teleoperation data more than doubled the mean success rate across eight evaluation conditions from 22.8% to 45.9%. Generalization to unseen object shapes and weights improved dramatically, demonstrating the power of scaling robot learning through human tactile demonstrations.
contributions: Developed a soft, durable capacitive tactile skin costing under $10 in materials per skin that conforms to differing human and robot hand geometries while maintaining a shared 202-taxel layout from fingertips to palm.
Quantitatively proved practical sensor durability through 10,000 cyclic loading-unloading tests, 1,280 tight-fist bending cycles, and motion artifact evaluations during finger flexion.

Formulated a human-robot co-training pipeline that incorporates human visuo-tactile demonstrations via an auxiliary language task phase prediction loss without requiring sensor-specific alignment mappings.

Demonstrated that adding human tactile demonstrations to a fixed budget of robot data improves the mean real-robot success rate across evaluation conditions, including out-of-distribution settings, from 22.8% to 45.9%.

sections.heading: Why Scaling Tactile Data Demands a Shared Skin for Humans and Robots
sections.summary: Tactile sensing is vital for contact-rich dexterous manipulation, but teleoperating robots to collect data is expensive. Leveraging cheaper human demonstrations requires a soft sensor that covers the entire hand of both humans and robots and yields structurally identical tactile signals. SoTa solves this with a soft tactile skin costing under $10 in materials.
sections.details:
Dexterous tasks like gently grasping a paper cup, wiping a table, or inserting a plug into an outlet require fine control over contacts across various regions of the hand. While vision alone can guide high-level motions, contact forces and slip cannot be observed directly by cameras, making tactile feedback essential.

However, teleoperating multi-fingered robot hands requires expensive rigs and remains difficult to scale. Collecting demonstrations directly with human hands offers an intuitive, scalable alternative. Yet existing tactile sensors have mostly been confined to fingertips or engineered strictly for specific robot hands, making it impossible to align signals between humans and robots. Effective human-robot co-training requires a tactile skin that covers the entire hand, conforms to diverse hand geometries, withstands repeated bending and contact, and shares an identical sensor layout across embodiments.

This paper introduces "SoTa" to bridge that gap. Built with a thin, multilayer conductive fabric design, SoTa customizes the outer geometry to fit human and robot hands while keeping the placement of 202 taxels identical across corresponding anatomical regions. Materials cost under $10 per skin. It retains over 97% of its initial response span after 10,000 loading cycles and withstands repeated tight-fist bending. This hardware standardization enables a single neural network to process both human and robot tactile inputs directly, drastically boosting policy generalization when modest robot data is augmented with human demonstrations.

sections.heading: The Evolution of Tactile Skins and Human-Robot Co-Training
sections.summary: Prior visuo-tactile policy learning has largely focused on fingertip sensors or parallel grippers, requiring complex cross-sensor representations to utilize human demonstrations. Tactile gloves are rarely portable to robot hands, and cross-embodiment devices often rely on rigid structures that restrict movement. SoTa provides full-hand soft skins with an identical taxel array across embodiments, enabling direct co-training without learned cross-sensor mappings.
sections.details:
To understand SoTa's place in the literature, we can look across three main research directions.

### Visuo-Tactile and Force-Controlled Policy Learning
Prior work has widely explored fusing vision with tactile or force feedback to enhance manipulation robustness. However, dexterous hand research has predominantly used fingertip-only sensors or sparse arrays of piezoresistive pads on the palm. Methods that incorporate human demonstrations have mostly been limited to single-finger force sensing or have relied on large cross-embodiment models (such as FTP-1) that require separate encoders for different sensors. SoTa builds upon the FTP-1 architecture, but by matching taxel layouts in hardware, it enables humans and robots to share a single tactile encoder directly.

### Tactile Interfaces for Dexterous Manipulation
While various tactile sensing technologies exist, including capacitive and magnetic approaches, high-density skins designed for robots are tailored to specific robot geometries, and human glove devices (like STAG or FlexGlove) are made strictly for human hands. A few cross-embodiment setups have been proposed, but they often impose rigid structures that hinder natural hand articulation or cover only fingertips and small palm patches. SoTa overcomes this dilemma by custom-profiling thin, soft skins that blanket the palm and all finger segments with 202 shared taxels.

### Human-Robot Co-Training Approaches
When learning from action-free human demonstrations, typical strategies involve retargeting hand poses to robot actions or setting up auxiliary objectives such as predicting future visual frames or 3D scene flow. For tactile data, previous approaches required paired human-robot data to align sensor representations. SoTa introduces an auxiliary loss that predicts language-based task phases from visuo-tactile features, naturally aligning human and robot representations without requiring paired demonstrations.

sections.heading: A $10 Soft Skin and an Unpaired Co-Training Architecture
sections.summary: SoTa is a capacitive tactile skin made from laser-micromachined conductive fabric and dielectric elastomer, sharing 202 taxels across human and robot hands. Robot teleoperation and human glove data are collected synchronously at 30 Hz. The policy extends the pre-trained FTP-1 model, using an auxiliary language expert that predicts manipulation phases to learn shared representations from action-free human demonstrations.
sections.details:
### III-A Sensor Design and Fabrication
SoTa customizes its outer layout to fit human and robot hand geometry while sharing the same capacitive sensing principle and taxel count. The 202 taxels are distributed across the hand: 40 on the thumb, 24 on the index finger, 16 on each of the middle, ring, and pinky fingers, and the remainder across the palm.

The multilayer stack is straightforward and practical. A 25 $\mu$m polyimide film is thermally bonded to an 80 $\mu$m conductive fabric using a 30 $\mu$m iron-on TPU film. An ultraviolet laser cuts the electrode patterns into the fabric. Two electrode layers sandwich a SEBS dielectric layer microstructured via sandpaper transfer molding, forming parallel-plate piezocapacitive sensors. The outer surfaces are encapsulated with soft SEBS and sealed with Kapton tape. Fabrication takes about 6 hours of laser micromachining and roughly 2 hours of manual assembly.

Signal processing is handled by a compact PCB housing an ESP32-S3 microcontroller and PCAP04 capacitance-to-digital converters, scanning all taxels at 30 fps. The human glove runs untethered for approximately 7 hours on a LiPo battery. Raw materials cost under $10 per skin, and the readout electronics cost around $30 in batches of 100.

### III-B Data Collection Setup
Both robot and human setups record visuo-tactile data at 30 Hz, using ZED Mini cameras for visual input and 202 taxels for touch.
- Robot setup: An operator controls the wrist pose of a Kinova arm with a Meta Quest controller and commands a Wuji dexterous hand with a Rokoko smart glove in real time.
- Human setup: The operator wears a fabric glove fitted with the SoTa skin and performs tasks naturally without a robot. The untethered design allows data collection outside the lab.
Both streams pass through an identical post-processing pipeline: baseline subtraction over the first 30 frames, spike filtering, normalization, and linear scaling from $[0.1, 2.0]$ to $[0, 1]$.

### III-C Policy Learning Architecture
The policy architecture builds upon FTP-1, a foundation model pre-trained on roughly 3,000 hours of diverse tactile data. It consists of a PaliGemma vision-language backbone, a tactile transformer, and a flow-matching action expert. Because sensor layouts match across embodiments, the tactile encoder is fully shared.

Human demonstrations lack robot joint commands (action labels). To leverage this data, SoTa incorporates an auxiliary "language expert" branch trained to predict the current task phase (e.g., "reach box", "rotate box", "release"). Training proceeds in two stages:
1. Representation pre-training: The vision-tactile backbone and language expert are trained on phase prediction using both human and robot demonstrations while the action branch is frozen.
2. Co-fine-tuning: The action expert's flow-matching loss on robot data and the language expert's auxiliary phase prediction loss on both human and robot data are optimized jointly. Human demonstrations never contribute to the action loss, preventing negative transfer.

sections.heading: Real-Robot Experiments: Tactile Benefits and Human-Driven Generalization
sections.summary: Evaluations across box reorientation, cup picking, and plug insertion showed that tactile feedback improved in-distribution success, but robot data alone struggled to generalize to unseen objects. Incorporating human visuo-tactile demonstrations in co-training doubled the average success rate across all eight conditions from 22.8% to 45.9%. The sensor also demonstrated exceptional electrical continuity in severe bending stress tests.
sections.details:
### IV-A Experimental Setup
The authors evaluated three manipulation tasks with distinct contact modes:
1. Box reorientation: Reorienting a box across the palm to target angles, involving extensive whole-hand contact.
2. Cup picking: Extracting the top paper cup from a tight stack without crushing it or dropping the stack, requiring delicate gripping force.
3. Plug insertion: Pinching an AC adapter with the fingers and inserting it into a wall outlet, demanding precise alignment under visual occlusion.

Robot training data was intentionally kept small, using only one object variant per task (75 demonstrations for box and plug, 50 for cup). Human training data included 150 demonstrations across three objects per task (one overlapping with the robot). Evaluations spanned three in-distribution (ID) conditions and five out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions featuring novel weights and shapes, running 40 unassisted trials per condition.

### IV-B Effect of Tactile Feedback
First, comparing vision-only ($\mathrm{R}^{\mathrm{V}}$) and visuo-tactile ($\mathrm{R}^{\mathrm{V},\mathrm{T}}$) policies trained solely on robot demonstrations revealed that tactile feedback consistently boosted ID performance (box: 50% to 67.5%, cup: 32.5% to 45%, plug: 0% to 17.5%). Under OOD conditions, however, performance either fell or remained at 0% for cups and plugs, even though box reorientation improved. Training on a single object caused the policy to overfit to object-specific local contact signatures.

### IV-C Human-Robot Co-Training and Auxiliary Learning
Introducing human visuo-tactile demonstrations via co-training ($\mathrm{R}^{\mathrm{V},\mathrm{T}}+\mathrm{H}^{\mathrm{V},\mathrm{T}}$) yielded dramatic improvements. The co-trained policy outperformed baselines across all eight test conditions (3 ID and 5 OOD), more than doubling the overall average success rate from 22.8% to 45.9%. Generalization under OOD conditions improved remarkably: rotating a 2.8x heavier box jumped from 32.5% to 70%, picking a novel square cup rose from 17.5% to 30%, and inserting a heavy charging brick climbed from 0% to 32.5%.

Ablation experiments confirmed that two-stage language training on robot data alone failed to achieve these OOD gains, and removing tactile signals from human data during co-training degraded performance. This shows that flowing human tactile experience across diverse objects directly into the network was the critical factor behind improved generalization.

### IV-D Durability and Motion Artifacts
In mechanical durability tests, sensor interconnects were attached across the index finger joint and subjected to repeated 180-degree tight-fist bending. Conventional FPCB (copper-on-polyimide) traces broke open after 80 cycles and silver paste traces failed after 640 cycles, whereas SoTa's conductive fabric traces maintained continuity after 1,280 cycles. Additionally, motion artifacts measured across four human subjects with different hand sizes during unconstrained flexion remained small (RMS 6.18%), equivalent to a contact load of about 0.2 N, confirming robust immunity to false touches.

sections.heading: Takeaways and Future Horizons: Democratizing Tactile Data
sections.summary: SoTa resolves the data scarcity bottleneck in tactile imitation learning by offering an inexpensive, durable tactile skin with a shared layout for humans and robots. Incorporating human demonstrations via auxiliary learning more than doubled manipulation generalization. Fabrication resources and firmware will be open-sourced, while scaling human data and studying long-term wear remain future work.
sections.details:
The central contribution of this work is demonstrating that hardware-level alignment can bridge the tactile gap between humans and robots, enabling scalable robot learning from inexpensive human demonstrations. Rather than requiring extensive teleoperation on costly multi-fingered robot hands, operators can collect diverse contact data simply by performing everyday tasks wearing untethered sensor gloves.

The authors note several limitations and directions for future research:
- Scaling human demonstration volume: The study used a fixed budget of 150 demonstrations per task; determining how performance scales with larger datasets and exploring how many robot demonstrations can be replaced by human data remains to be explored.
- Comparative study on layout alignment: A direct comparison between hardware-aligned taxel layouts and learned cross-sensor mappings has not yet been performed.
- Long-term mechanical wear: While the sensor passed 10,000 load cycles and 1,280 bending cycles, evaluation under long-term abrasive friction encountered in prolonged daily manipulation remains open.

All fabrication workflows, CAD designs, PCB Gerber files, and firmware for SoTa will be released as open source. Democratizing access to compliant tactile skins will help accelerate data-driven dexterous manipulation research.

takeaways: Aligning tactile sensor layouts in hardware enables human-robot co-training with a single shared encoder, bypassing complex cross-sensor mapping models.

While robot-only tactile policies tend to overfit to specific object shapes, augmenting them with human tactile demonstrations on varied objects dramatically improves out-of-distribution generalization.
Laser-micromachined conductive fabric electrodes achieve an ultra-low material cost under $10 per skin alongside high mechanical durability, surviving over 1,000 severe joint bending cycles.
limitations: The minimum ratio of robot demonstrations required before substituting them with human data has not been fully explored.
The feasibility of shared layouts has not been evaluated on hands with substantially different finger counts or proportions.
Long-term resistance to surface elastomer delamination and abrasive wear under continuous frictional contact remains to be characterized.
